summary: For ages 6–7 (UK Year 2; in the US this content is formally taught in Grade 3, usually ages 8–9): teach that multiplication is commutative (a×b = b×a) by rotating an array so the same objects give the same total read two ways, use this to nearly halve fact-learning, and firmly teach the boundary that division is NOT commutative (12÷3 ≠ 3÷12) to prevent over-generalising. Learners should predict then prove commutativity by action, use it as a strategy to derive and check facts, and refute the claim that order never matters.
misconceptions: Over-generalising commutativity to division and subtraction (thinking 12÷3 = 3÷12, or 8−3 = 3−8).
Believing 3×4 and 4×3 are different facts needing separate memorisation.
Accepting commutativity as a stated rule without being able to justify it (no array reasoning).
Confusing 'same product' with 'same situation' — not seeing that different stories can share an answer.
Applying commutativity correctly to × but then assuming order never matters in any calculation.

activities.title: Predict then rotate the array to prove 3×4 = 4×3
steps: Build an array of 3 rows of 4 counters (or dots) and count the total: 12.
Before you turn the array, predict whether the total will change if you turn it, and give your reason.
Rotate the whole array a quarter turn so it becomes 4 rows of 3 — do not add or remove any counters.
Count again and confirm the total is still 12; record 3×4 = 4×3.
Repeat with another pair you choose (e.g. 2×5 and 5×2) and state the matching fact.
Explain in your own words WHY the total cannot change when you turn the array.
activities.insight: The same set of objects, read in two directions, gives the same product, so multiplication can be done in either order — this is predicted and then seen by rotating, not merely stated as a rule.

activities.title: Use commutativity to get facts for free
steps: Given a known fact (e.g. 3×8 = 24), state its commuted partner (8×3 = 24) without recomputing.
Look at a multiplication square and find the diagonal line of symmetry; notice that facts on either side of it mirror each other.
Decide which of a pair is easier to work out (e.g. 2×9 vs 9×2) and explain why using the easier order helps.
Use 'compute both ways and compare' to check one of your own answers.
activities.insight: Because order doesn't matter for multiplication, each known fact gives its partner free, nearly halving the facts to learn, and you can pick the easier order or check your work.

activities.title: Test the boundary: division does not swap
steps: Act out 12 ÷ 3 with counters: share 12 counters into 3 equal groups and count one group (4).
Now act out 3 ÷ 12: try to share 3 counters among 12 — you cannot give everyone a whole counter, so each would get less than one.
Compare the two results and state clearly that 12÷3 ≠ 3÷12 (4 is not the same as less than one).
Try to 'rotate' the sharing the way you rotated a multiplication array, and describe why it does not work.
Decide for each pair whether order can swap: sort statements (mixing × and ÷) into 'order can swap' and 'order matters'.
Consider whether swapping works for subtraction too (e.g. 8−3 vs 3−8) and say what you find.
activities.insight: Multiplication's array can be turned freely without changing the total, but swapping the two numbers in a division (or subtraction) usually changes the answer (it only stays the same when the two numbers are equal) — so the swapping shortcut has a precise stopping point.

activities.title: Same product, different story
steps: Draw or set out '3 bags of 4' and '4 bags of 3' as two separate situations.
Confirm both give 12, then explain how the stories differ even though the answer is the same.
Match a context picture to the fact it shows, and to its commuted partner.
activities.insight: Different real situations can share the same product; 'same answer' is not the same as 'same story'.

activities.title: Refute the character who says division swaps too
steps: Listen to a character claim 'division works both ways, like multiplication — 12÷3 is the same as 3÷12'.
Disagree and give a counterexample, backing it up by sharing counters both ways.
State the correct rule: multiplication can be swapped, division cannot.
activities.insight: You can justify and defend the boundary of commutativity by producing a worked counterexample, not just asserting it.

checkQuestion: Is 3 × 5 the same as 5 × 3? And is 12 ÷ 3 the same as 3 ÷ 12? For each one, tell me yes or no and how you know.
checkAnswer: 3 × 5 = 5 × 3 (both 15) — it's the same array turned on its side, so multiplication can be done in either order. But 12 ÷ 3 (= 4) is NOT the same as 3 ÷ 12 (less than one) — division can't be swapped round.
